title: Exceed the Standard
author: Xinli Wang, Michelle Davidson and Jamie de Jong
summary: This guest post from three University of Manitoba mathematics instructors describes moving a 300-student general mathematics course, MATH1010, to standards-based grading after years of high fail and withdrawal rates. They narrowed the course to 20 learning outcomes, tested each outcome two or three times before the final, and scored every attempt as simply mastered or not yet, with the final grade set by the number of outcomes mastered. Feedback is delivered through Crowdmark, and tests are returned in time for students to reattempt. In the first term 33 percent of students earned an A or A+, against 15.4 percent in the prior three years, and the fail or withdrawal rate fell from 49.2 to 34.7 percent. The authors are candid about the heavy up-front workload and list the supports that made it workable, including grade spreadsheets, a comment library and a problem bank.
points: Standards-based grading with a small set of clear learning outcomes and a mastery-or-not-yet scale gave struggling students room to reattempt without penalty.
Results improved markedly: A grades more than doubled and the fail or withdrawal rate fell from 49.2 to 34.7 percent, without making the course easier.
Fast, specific feedback returned before the next test is what lets students incorporate comments when they retry an outcome.
The workload is front-loaded, and tools such as a grading spreadsheet, a comment library and a problem bank make it sustainable.
quotes: Generally, this has left a bi-modal distribution with a high failure rate.

When a student attempts questions from a learning outcome, they either earn a grade of 0, indicating that mastery was not shown, or a grade of 1, indicating that mastery was shown. Once they have demonstrated mastery for a learning outcome, they don’t need to attempt it on any subsequent tests.
We were able to find a schedule for the term that allowed each learning outcome to be tested 2 or 3 times prior to the final exam.
Our goal is to return the tests approximately 5-6 days after the test, with at least 2 days before any learning outcomes are retested.

In Fall 2025, 33% of students earned an A or A+, compared with an average of 15.4% in the 3 years prior. Since an A requires students to have mastered at least 17 of the 20 learning outcomes in the course, we do not feel that the course has been made easier, but rather that the students have achieved more.

From an instructor perspective, many students made the most of the system, and seemed to thrive in the course. Students worked hard to attain the grades they aimed for, and took responsibility for planning for assessments.

The initial workload was high, to define the learning outcomes, nail down how questions were designed, and create many questions. However, it has also been a very rewarding experience, as we can shift our focus from discussion over part marks, to students’ learning.
